Single-cell and spatial transcriptome analyses unveil that MYH11 links stemness to immunotherapy resistance in non-small cell lung cancer.

Using single-cell RNA sequencing combined with spatial transcriptomics in non-small cell lung cancer, the authors identify a stemness-high tumor subpopulation marked by elevated MYH11 expression. They link this MYH11-high stemness program to immunotherapy resistance, suggesting a potential biomarker or target for overcoming treatment failure.

Spatial transcriptomics reveals PDIA6 as a tumor-intrinsic driver of mesenchymal plasticity and vascular microenvironment remodeling in glioblastoma.

Using spatial transcriptomics, this study identifies PDIA6 as a tumor-intrinsic factor in glioblastoma that promotes mesenchymal plasticity and remodels the vascular microenvironment, potentially creating protective perivascular niches. The findings link PDIA6 to malignant-endothelial crosstalk and suggest it as a candidate driver of therapy resistance.

Lineage-mixed neurodevelopmental programs in pediatric sarcomas nominate tumor-selective surface antigen pairs.

The authors analyzed a pan-pediatric single-cell RNA-seq atlas of 266 samples across 22 pediatric solid tumor types to identify shared developmental gene expression programs. They found that these tumors exhibit lineage-mixed neurodevelopmental programs, which they used to nominate tumor-selective surface antigen pairs as potential therapeutic targets. This work demonstrates how convergent developmental biology across pediatric cancers can reveal shared vulnerabilities.

HOMED enables hierarchical and multimodal optimization of DNA methylation deconvolution across tissues.

HOMED is a new computational framework for DNA methylation deconvolution that accounts for hierarchical relationships among related cell types, uses single-cell RNA-seq to guide signature selection, and leverages paired bulk RNA-seq/DNAm data to optimize CpG signatures. This improves cell-type composition estimation from bulk methylation data across tissues, addressing a key confounder in epigenome-wide association studies.

Categorization and analysis of 16 computational methods for estimating cell potency from single-cell RNA-seq data.

This review categorizes 16 computational methods for estimating cell potency (differentiation potential) from static scRNA-seq data into average-based, entropy-based, and knowledge-based approaches. The authors analyze the contrasting assumptions underlying these methods and evaluate them on a unified mathematical framework. The work provides guidance for choosing appropriate potency estimation tools and highlights how methodological assumptions shape biological interpretation.

CellMarker 3.0: an updated resource of manually curated and computationally predicted cell markers in human/mouse and interactive web tools for single-cell and spatial transcriptomics analysis.

CellMarker 3.0 is an updated database that combines manually curated, experimentally validated cell marker genes with computationally predicted markers for many cell types across human and mouse tissues. It adds substantial new content over the prior version (274 tissues, 1,877 cell types, 64,040 markers, and over 1.2 million tissue-cell type-marker entries) and introduces interactive web tools for analyzing single-cell RNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics data.

Overlapping yet distinct spatiomolecular profiles across mood disorders and biological sex in the human prefrontal cortex.

This study used spatial transcriptomics on human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex to compare molecular profiles in major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, and neurotypical controls, focusing on differences by diagnosis and biological sex. It found overlapping yet distinct spatiomolecular signatures across mood disorders, with sex-specific molecular programs, revealing how clinical similarities and sex differences are reflected at the cellular and molecular level in the brain.

Overcoming segmentation bottlenecks in brain tissue for spatial proteomic inference at population scale.

The authors present SPInfer, a workflow for spatial proteomic inference that addresses the challenge of accurate cell segmentation in morphologically complex human brain tissue. Using 5,832 manually annotated cell bodies from 120 immunofluorescence images of the prefrontal cortex, they benchmark eight segmentation methods and show how domain adaptation affects downstream discovery at population scale.

spaTransfer: transfer learning for single-cell and spatial transcriptomics data using non-negative matrix factorization.

spaTransfer is a new computational method that uses non-negative matrix factorization to transfer cell type and spatial domain annotations from a reference single-cell or spatial transcriptomics atlas to new target samples. It is designed to handle the common real-world challenge where reference and target data differ in resolution or were generated on different experimental platforms. This enables researchers to leverage existing annotated atlases to label new spatial and single-cell datasets without re-annotating from scratch.

Denoising single-cell ATAC-seq data with Shannon entropy.

The authors introduce a Shannon entropy-based method for denoising scATAC-seq data by identifying and filtering out low-quality droplets (empty, damaged nuclei, or debris) that can distort downstream analyses. Unlike existing approaches that rely on read depth or predefined genomic features, this method uses the information content of chromatin accessibility profiles to distinguish high-quality nuclei. This helps preserve rare cell populations that might otherwise be obscured by noisy droplets.

CellWHISPER disentangles direct cell-cell communication from structural proximity.

CellWHISPER is a new computational framework for inferring direct, contact-dependent cell-cell communication (gap junctions and ligand-receptor signaling) from spatial transcriptomics data. It addresses the high error rates of existing tools by using a statistical procedure that controls for confounding effects of cell-type-specific expression and spatial organization, with closed-form significance scores that scale to large datasets.

Spatial proximity to AD pathology defines cell-type and genotype-specific characteristics in human AD hippocampus.

This study developed a spatial transcriptomics pipeline combining MERFISH with concurrent annotation of amyloid-β plaques and AT8 phosphorylated tau pathology in human control and Alzheimer's disease hippocampus. They identified cell-type-specific expression signatures in glia and neurons based on proximity to Aβ plaques, tau-enriched neurons, or both pathologies combined, and used these spatially defined signatures to infer pathology-associated states in large snRNA-seq datasets. The work links spatial proximity to AD pathology with cell-type and genotype-specific transcriptional responses.

Thermodynamic Quality Control Reshapes Spatially Resolved Metabolic Flux Predictions in Prostate Cancer.

This study integrates spatial transcriptomics from twelve regions of a single prostate tumor with a genome-scale metabolic model (Human-GEM) using an E-Flux framework, adding nutrient constraints and explicit thermodynamic cycle certification via loopless flux variability analysis. The authors show that failing to eliminate thermodynamically infeasible cycles (TICs) substantially distorts spatially resolved metabolic flux predictions, and that enforcing thermodynamic quality control reshapes those predictions across normal, inflamed, and Gleason 3+3/3+4 tissue regions.

X-SPEAR: An Extensible Framework for Spatial Panel Evaluation and Refinement.

X-SPEAR is a framework for designing and evaluating gene panels for targeted spatial transcriptomics platforms like 10x Xenium, addressing the problem that genes detected in scRNA-seq references are often detected in fewer cells in the spatial assay. Its DART method learns short Boolean gene rules and retains multiple gene-disjoint rules per cell type to improve rare-cell typing. The tool helps researchers check and refine panels before committing to costly spatial experiments.

Survival-associated cellular communication networks in human solid cancers.

The authors developed SKyNet, a method that integrates single-cell RNA-seq cell-cell communication networks with bulk RNA-seq and clinical survival data from TCGA across 11 solid cancers. By combining a pan-cancer atlas of 318,426 cells and 78 cell types, SKyNet identifies ligand-receptor interactions whose predicted communication strength is associated with overall survival, revealing cancer-type-specific communication signatures with clinical relevance.

KLRB1 (CD161) as a context-dependent prognostic marker in breast cancer: An exploratory analysis of CD4+ memory T cell infiltration: a retrospective multi-cohort study.

This retrospective multi-cohort study examined whether KLRB1 (CD161) expression predicts outcomes in breast cancer and whether CD4+ memory T cell abundance modifies that relationship, integrating TCGA, METABRIC, single-cell RNA-seq, spatial transcriptomics, and multiplex immunofluorescence data. The analysis suggests KLRB1's prognostic value is context-dependent, varying with CD4+ memory T cell infiltration rather than acting as a uniform marker. As an exploratory study, it proposes a cell-context framework for interpreting this immune marker but does not establish clinical utility.

PIANO enables generative modeling of gene expression and scales multi-omics integration to 100 million cells.

PIANO is a deep learning framework that uses a generative model of gene expression to integrate single-cell multi-omics data. It addresses three key challenges: correcting strong batch effects, scaling to millions of cells (up to 100 million), and modeling how covariates influence expression. This enables more accurate and scalable integration of large transcriptomic atlases.

SigBridgeR: An R Toolkit for Standardized Identification and Benchmarking of Phenotype-Associated Cell Subpopulations in Single-Cell Transcriptomics.

SigBridgeR is an R toolkit that standardizes the identification and benchmarking of phenotype-associated cell subpopulations by integrating bulk transcriptomic and single-cell RNA-seq data. It addresses the current fragmentation in the field—where different algorithms, parameters, and output formats make fair comparison and reproducibility difficult—by providing a unified framework for running and evaluating multiple methods. This enables researchers to more reliably determine which approach best links cell subpopulations to clinical phenotypes.

Gene Expression Nebulas 2.0: an updated resource of gene expression profiles by incorporating more datasets, annotations, and functionalities.

Disagreement-informed arbitration for gene regulatory network inference: A score-level meta-classifier and a diagnostic typology of inter-method conflict.

The authors propose a per-edge arbitration approach for gene regulatory network inference, training a gradient-boosted classifier on the raw scores from ten different inference methods so that method weighting varies by edge rather than being fixed globally. They also introduce a diagnostic typology of inter-method conflicts. This addresses the common problem that different inference methods disagree on individual edges, which practitioners typically resolve by picking one method or averaging all of them.

A categorization of spatial transcriptomics methods for cell-cell communication analysis.

This review categorizes 33 recent computational methods for inferring cell-cell communication from spatial transcriptomics data into three groups: cell-type or single-cell resolution network inference, modeling of microenvironment-driven transcriptional variability, and regulatory modulation. It highlights how spatial context enables more biologically grounded communication inference than single-cell RNA-seq alone, and maps methods to the distinct biological questions they address.

A contextual activity score (CAS) for inferring ADAR-associated transcriptional activity across RNA-seq, single-cell, and spatial transcriptomics.

The framework aims to enable broader inference of ADAR activity in technologies where read-level editing quantification is impractical.

Residual disease as a therapy-remodeled ecosystem: spatial niches, tumor persistence, and relapse in solid tumors.

This narrative review argues that residual disease after cancer therapy should be viewed as a therapy-remodeled ecosystem rather than simply a smaller version of the original tumor. It links treatment-induced changes in the tissue environment—cell death, inflammation, repair, stromal activation, vascular injury, and metabolic stress—to where surviving tumor cells persist and when relapse-directed interventions might be most effective. The authors caution that spatial co-localization of residual cells with certain tissue features does not by itself prove a protective niche.

Immune-chondrocyte ligand-receptor axes in osteoarthritis: microenvironmental control of inflammation, matrix remodeling, and chondrocyte fate.

This narrative review synthesizes evidence that ligand-receptor communication between immune cells and chondrocytes drives osteoarthritis progression, translating inflammatory and mechanical microenvironmental cues into disease-relevant chondrocyte phenotypes. It catalogs major cytokine and other immune-derived signaling axes (e.g., IL-1β-IL-1R, TNF-α-TNFR) that regulate inflammation, matrix remodeling, and chondrocyte fate. The review frames OA as a whole-joint disease rather than simple cartilage wear, emphasizing intercellular crosstalk as a therapeutic target.
